subtitle: JavaScript runs one thing at a time, yet handles clicks, timers and network replies. The event loop is the trick.

lang.body:
JavaScript was written in ten days, and you can feel it: brilliant ideas next to a few odd corners. Let’s learn the safe path through it. For variables use let and const (block-scoped; prefer const). The types are number, string, boolean, null, undefined, object, array and function. Functions are values, so you can pass them around: const add = (a, b) => a + b.

Here is the corner to avoid. Use ===, not ==, to avoid coercion surprises, since 0 == '0' is true. So 0 === "0" is false: different types never match under ===.
keynotes: Variables use let and const (block-scoped; prefer const).
Types: number, string, boolean, null, undefined, object, array and function; functions are values, as in const add = (a, b) => a + b.

dom.body:
Picture the page as a family tree of objects, and your code as someone who can reach into any branch and change it. That tree is the DOM. document.querySelector('#btn') finds a node; el.textContent = … changes it; el.addEventListener('click', fn) reacts.

There is a clever behaviour you can use: events bubble up from the target to ancestors, like a ripple travelling up the tree. So one listener on a list can handle all its items (event delegation), instead of attaching hundreds of listeners. Event bubbling means an event travels from the target up through its ancestors.
keynotes: The DOM is the page as a tree of objects: querySelector finds a node, textContent changes it and addEventListener reacts.
Events bubble up from the target to ancestors.
One listener on a list can handle all its items (event delegation).

loop.body:
Here is a puzzle. JavaScript can only do one thing at a time, yet your page responds to clicks while a timer runs and an image downloads. How? Think of a single waiter in a restaurant who never stands waiting at the kitchen door: he takes an order, hands it to the kitchen, and moves on.

JavaScript has one call stack. Slow work (timers, network, I/O) is handed to the browser; when it finishes, a callback is queued. The event loop moves a queued callback onto the stack only when the stack is empty. Microtasks (promise callbacks) run before the next macrotask (timer, event). So `setTimeout(f, 0); console.log("a")` prints “a” first: a 0 ms timer still waits for the stack to empty, as the figure shows.
keynotes: JavaScript has one call stack; slow work is handed to the browser and a callback is queued when it finishes.
The event loop moves a queued callback onto the stack only when the stack is empty.
Microtasks (promise callbacks) run before the next macrotask (timer, event); a 0 ms timer still waits for the stack to empty.

async.body:
Waiting is the main thing a web page does: for a server, a file, a user. A Promise represents a future value: pending → fulfilled or rejected, like a restaurant pager that buzzes when your food is ready. And await pauses an async function (not the thread) until the promise settles: const res = await fetch(url); const data = await res.json();.

Handle failure with try/catch, and run independent requests together with Promise.all. See the saving: two independent requests take 300 ms and 200 ms. Sequentially that is 500 ms; with Promise.all it is the max of the two, 300 ms. Never wait for one if you can wait for both at once.
keynotes: A Promise represents a future value: pending, then fulfilled or rejected.
await pauses an async function (not the thread) until the promise settles; handle failure with try/catch.
Two independent requests of 300 ms and 200 ms take 500 ms sequentially but 300 ms with Promise.all.

fetch.body:
Now you can put it all together. A click handler calls fetch('/api/items'), awaits JSON and updates the DOM, and there is no page reload. That is the whole trick behind most modern web apps, and it is the idea in the figure.

One security rule gets in your way until you understand it: the browser’s same-origin policy blocks reading responses from other origins unless the server allows it via CORS headers. CORS is a rule enforced by the browser, not by the server.
keynotes: A click handler can call fetch('/api/items'), await JSON and update the DOM with no page reload.
The same-origin policy blocks reading responses from other origins unless the server allows it via CORS headers.
CORS is enforced by the browser.

spa.body:
As interfaces grow, updating the DOM by hand becomes a mess of bugs. Frameworks (React, Vue, Svelte) offer a calmer way: describe the UI as a function of state. Change the state and the framework updates only the DOM parts that differ (virtual DOM or fine-grained reactivity).

A few habits will serve you well: keep state minimal, derive the rest, and lift shared state up to the nearest common parent. In a component framework, the UI is a function of the state.
keynotes: Frameworks (React, Vue, Svelte) describe the UI as a function of state.
Changing the state updates only the DOM parts that differ.
Keep state minimal, derive the rest, and lift shared state up to the nearest common parent.
